drills.q: Explain TrueTime and commit-wait together, mechanically, in the order Spanner actually executes them.
drills.a: At commit time, Spanner picks a timestamp T inside the interval [earliest, latest] TrueTime.now() returns (uncertainty typically under 7ms, backed by GPS + atomic clocks). Before exposing the transaction's writes to any reader, Spanner performs commit-wait: it blocks until TrueTime guarantees real time has definitely passed T everywhere. This ordering trick -- picking inside an uncertainty window then waiting out the remainder of that uncertainty -- is what lets Spanner guarantee any transaction that committed earlier in real wall-clock time gets a provably smaller timestamp than one starting later, globally, without a central sequencer or global lock.

drills.q: A team migrates build-artifact buckets rebuilt weekly to Coldline storage to save money, and the bill goes up. Diagnose.
drills.a: Coldline has a 90-day minimum storage duration -- deleting or overwriting an object before 90 days elapses still bills the full 90-day minimum period. Weekly-churned artifacts get charged for 90 days of storage each, which can exceed what Standard (no minimum) would have cost. Fix: keep high-churn data on Standard, or use Autoclass which avoids the early-deletion fee for auto-migrated objects (though the fix here is really 'don't tier data that churns faster than the minimum duration').

drills.q: Compare Spanner's external consistency to Aurora Global Database and Cosmos DB Strong consistency. Why can't either substitute for Spanner?
drills.a: Aurora Global replicates asynchronously to secondary regions with real (if typically small) replica lag and no bounded, guaranteed ordering across regions -- it's not externally consistent. Cosmos DB Strong consistency uses quorum reads (2x RU cost) but is architected around single-region-authoritative writes with configurable multi-region consistency, not TrueTime-style global commit-wait across multi-region writes. Neither gives globally distributed multi-region WRITE availability combined with real-time (wall-clock-matching) global ordering the way Spanner's TrueTime + commit-wait does.

drills.q: Design a Bigtable row key for millions of IoT devices reporting every few seconds, and state the tradeoff your design makes.
drills.a: Naive timestamp#device_id hot-spots the tablet owning the newest time range. Better: device_id#reverse_timestamp -- spreads writes across the key space by leading with high-cardinality device_id, keeps per-device time-range scans (latest-first) efficient via reverse timestamp. Tradeoff: this sacrifices efficient global time-window scans across ALL devices at once, since device_id-first ordering scatters same-timestamp rows for different devices across the key space -- the schema has to pick per-device or global-time-window as the primary access pattern.

drills.q: Why can't Bigtable support a 'transfer funds between two accounts' operation correctly, regardless of row-key design?
drills.a: Bigtable gives strong consistency only for single-row read-modify-write operations (counters, single-entity atomic updates) and has no multi-row ACID transaction support at all. A funds transfer needs an atomic decrement on one row and increment on another to succeed or fail together -- that's a cross-row transactional guarantee Bigtable's data model simply doesn't offer, no row-key redesign fixes it. This needs Spanner (or Cloud SQL/AlloyDB if global scale isn't required) instead.

drills.q: Explain Spanner interleaved tables and how a wrong interleave hierarchy recreates the hot-split problem Spanner is supposed to solve.
drills.a: Interleaving physically co-locates a child table's rows with its parent row on the same split (e.g. Orders interleaved in Customers on CustomerId), so transactions/reads spanning parent and child stay within one split instead of a distributed multi-split operation. If the child is high-write-volume and the parent key has low cardinality or one hot value, ALL of that child's writes concentrate onto whichever split holds the hot parent -- the exact horizontal-scale-defeating hot-split problem Spanner's architecture is meant to avoid, just recreated via bad schema design instead of bad primary-key design.

drills.q: When should a team pick AlloyDB over both Cloud SQL and BigQuery for a workload needing both transactional and analytical access?
drills.a: AlloyDB fits when analytical queries need to run against LIVE transactional data with low staleness tolerance and the analytical scale doesn't require BigQuery's massively parallel serverless engine -- the columnar engine gives up to 100x faster scans on the current operational dataset without a separate ETL pipeline. It's the wrong choice once analytics is genuinely warehouse-scale (many-TB historical aggregation, ad-hoc analyst queries across full history) -- at that point ETL/CDC into BigQuery and accepting staleness is the better fit, since a single AlloyDB instance's columnar engine accelerates live-data scans, not multi-year historical aggregation at BigQuery's scale.

drills.q: A Cloud SQL instance is approaching 60TB with degrading backup and failover times. Walk through the real options in order of increasing architectural change.
drills.a: 1) Archive/cold-tier historical data out of the primary instance to shrink it below the degradation zone -- cheapest, least disruptive. 2) Shard across multiple Cloud SQL instances at the application layer -- real complexity, no platform support. 3) Migrate to AlloyDB if the Aurora-style separated-storage architecture alone (without needing Spanner's global-consistency machinery) solves the ceiling -- moderate migration effort. 4) Migrate to Spanner if the actual underlying need is horizontal write scale with strong consistency, not just more storage headroom -- highest effort, only justified if requirement 4 is real.

drills.q: A candidate says 'Spanner is just Cloud SQL that auto-shards.' What's the precise correction?
drills.a: Sharding alone -- splitting data across nodes -- doesn't give cross-shard ACID transactions with global ordering; plenty of sharded relational setups (Citus, manually-sharded MySQL) exist without that guarantee. Spanner's actual differentiator is combining horizontal sharding WITH TrueTime-backed external consistency, giving cross-shard, cross-region ACID transactions that behave, from an ordering perspective, as if they ran on a single machine. That combination -- not sharding by itself -- is what nothing else offers directly.

drills.q: Design the storage-class lifecycle for a media company's user-uploaded video, and explain the failure mode of over-aggressive early tiering.
drills.a: Standard for the first ~30 days (high view probability, no retrieval fee). Nearline (30-day min, $0.01/GB retrieval) as views decline. Coldline (90-day min, $0.02/GB retrieval) once views are minimal. Archive (365-day min, $0.05/GB retrieval) for long-term retention with near-zero access. Autoclass in practice beats hand-tuned age thresholds since real view-decay curves rarely match a clean schedule. Failure mode: a video moved to Coldline unexpectedly goes viral -- the $0.02/GB retrieval fee applies per access and can dwarf the storage savings at high view volume on a large file; Autoclass's per-object monitoring catches and reverses this automatically, a static lifecycle rule would not until the next scheduled review.

drills.q: Why is NTP-synchronized clock uncertainty insufficient to replicate Spanner's guarantees outside Google's infrastructure?
drills.a: NTP-only synchronization typically leaves clock uncertainty in the tens-to-hundreds of milliseconds range, versus TrueTime's under-7ms bound from GPS receivers and atomic clocks cross-checked in every datacenter. Commit-wait's cost scales directly with the uncertainty bound being waited out -- at NTP-scale uncertainty, commit-wait would either add unacceptable per-transaction latency or force accepting a materially weaker consistency guarantee than Spanner's. This is why TrueTime-grade external consistency is a genuine infrastructure moat, not just a software technique anyone can replicate by copying the commit-wait algorithm.

drills.q: Explain why Bigtable and BigQuery are often used together for the same clickstream dataset rather than picking one.
drills.a: Bigtable serves the ingestion/serving path: extremely high write throughput, low-latency single-key lookups (e.g. a user's last N events by user_id), no ad-hoc analytical query need. BigQuery serves the analysis path: ad-hoc SQL aggregation, joins, scan-based billing suited to occasional large queries rather than constant point lookups. Bigtable has no SQL engine or secondary indexes, so analytical queries beyond a row-key range scan require either a slow client-side full scan or BigQuery's external Bigtable connector -- worse than querying data already loaded natively into BigQuery. A pipeline (Dataflow) continuously loads the same stream into both, accepting the duplication as the right tradeoff.
